title: Boosting III — XGBoost

blocks.t: From the notes
XGBoost, as the notes frame it
XGBoost = Extreme Gradient Boosting.
It is gradient boosting plus improvements:

items: Regularization — it has a penalty term inside the objective itself.
Handles missing values on its own.

blocks.t: The tree is built using the Similarity Score and the Gain:
A split is kept only if $\textbf{Gain} - \boldsymbol{\gamma} > 0$.

Everything in Topic 67 still holds — start from a constant, fit trees to
residuals, add them shrunk by $\lambda_{\text{lr}}$. XGBoost changes only
how each individual tree is grown. Ordinary gradient boosting grows the
tree with plain MSE on the residuals; XGBoost grows it with a criterion derived
directly from the loss it is actually minimising, including the regularisation
penalty. That is why the splitting rule looks different: it is not a heuristic,
it falls out of the algebra.
Deriving the similarity score
At round $t$ the objective over $n$ rows is

\mathcal{L}^{(t)} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} L \left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i)\right)
 + \Omega(f_t),
\qquad
\Omega(f)=\gamma T + \tfrac12 \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{T} w_j^2 ,

where $T$ is the number of leaves and $w_j$ the value in leaf $j$. Take a
second-order Taylor expansion of $L$ around $\hat y^{(t-1)}$, writing
$g_i=\partial_{\hat y} L$ and $h_i=\partial^2_{\hat y} L$:

\mathcal{L}^{(t)} \simeq \sum_i \Big[ g_i f_t(x_i) + \tfrac12 h_i f_t(x_i)^2 \Big]
+ \gamma T + \tfrac12\lambda\sum_j w_j^2 .

Every row in leaf $j$ gets the same output $w_j$, so group by leaf with
$G_j=\sum_{i\in j} g_i$ and $H_j=\sum_{i\in j} h_i$:
\mathcal{L}^{(t)} \simeq \sum_{j=1}^{T}\Big[G_j w_j + \tfrac12 (H_j+\lambda) w_j^2\Big] + \gamma T .

This is a quadratic in $w_j$. Setting the derivative to zero gives the
optimal leaf weight and the resulting objective value:

The quantity $\dfrac{G_j^2}{H_j+\lambda}$ is exactly the notes'
similarity score: for squared loss $g_i=-(y_i-\hat y_i)=-r_i$ and
$h_i=1$, so $G_j^2 = (\sum r)^2$ and $H_j = n$, giving
\text{Similarity}=\frac{(\sum \text{residuals})^2}{n+\lambda}. \checkmark
Splitting a node into left and right changes $\mathcal{L}^\star$ by

\boxed{ \text{Gain}=\tfrac12\left[\frac{G_L^2}{H_L+\lambda}+\frac{G_R^2}{H_R+\lambda}
-\frac{(G_L+G_R)^2}{H_L+H_R+\lambda}\right]-\gamma }

which is the notes' $\text{Sim}_L+\text{Sim}_R-\text{Sim}_{\text{root}}$, and the
$-\gamma$ is the notes' pruning rule "keep the split only if
$\text{Gain}-\gamma>0$".

Notice what $\lambda$ does in the denominator. A leaf holding few rows has a
small $H_j$, so $\lambda$ dominates and both the similarity score and the leaf
weight are pulled towards zero. Regularisation therefore hurts small,
noisy leaves far more than large confident ones — exactly the behaviour we
want, and it comes free from the algebra rather than being bolted on.

blocks.t: A worked split, by hand

The root similarity is zero here because the residuals sum to
zero — which they always do at the first round, since the initial prediction
is the mean. That is not a coincidence: it means the first split's gain is
purely the sum of the two child similarities, i.e. a measure of how cleanly
the split separates positive from negative residuals.

Similarity is $(\sum r)^2$, not $\sum r^2$. Residuals that cancel
produce a low score. A node containing $+5$ and $-5$ scores
$0$, while a node containing $+5$ and $+5$ scores $100/(2+\lambda)$. This is
the point: a node is "pure" for XGBoost when its residuals point the
same way, because then one leaf value can fix all of them at once.

Typical
What it does
rows: Shrinkage per tree. Same role as in Topic 67.
$L_2$ on leaf weights — the $\lambda$ in the similarity denominator.
$L_1$ on leaf weights; can zero a leaf out entirely.
Minimum gain required to keep a split. The notes' pruning term.
Minimum $\sum h_i$ in a child. For log loss $h=p(1-p)$, so this means "a leaf needs enough uncertain rows".
Reweights the positive class for imbalance.
Histogram binning — the big speed win.

blocks.t:
Two different $\lambda$s. The notes use $\lambda$ for the learning rate
in plain gradient boosting and $\lambda$ appears as the $L_2$ term in the
similarity score. They are different parameters. In the library they are
learning_rate and reg_lambda. Keep them apart.
Why it is fast, and why it handles NaN

Histogram binning. Exact split finding must sort every feature and try
every threshold: $O(n\log n)$ per feature per node. tree_method="hist"
buckets each feature into 256 bins once, up front; thereafter finding the best
split is a single pass accumulating $G$ and $H$ per bin. That turns the inner
loop from sorting into adding.

Column blocks. Data is stored pre-sorted in compressed column blocks
that are reused across every tree, so the sorting cost is paid once for the
whole run rather than once per node.

Parallelism. Boosting is sequential across trees — tree $t+1$ needs
tree $t$'s residuals. But within one tree, the search over features for
the best split is embarrassingly parallel. That is what n_jobs
parallelises. Anyone who says "XGBoost parallelises boosting" has it wrong.

Sparsity awareness. For every split XGBoost learns a default
direction. Rows with a missing value for that feature are sent that way. It
tries both directions during training and keeps whichever gives more gain. So
missingness is treated as information, not as something to paper over with an
imputer.

blocks.t: Code

import numpy as np
import xgboost as xgb
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=6000, n_features=25, n_informative=10,
                           weights=[0.8, 0.2], random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25,
                                      stratify=y, random_state=0)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. THE SKLEARN-STYLE API  (use this 95% of the time)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
clf = xgb.XGBClassifier(
        n_estimators      = 2000,      # upper bound; early stopping decides
        learning_rate     = 0.05,      # eta
        max_depth         = 5,
        min_child_weight  = 5,         # min sum of hessians in a child
        gamma             = 0.5,       # the notes' pruning term
        reg_lambda        = 2.0,       # L2 -- the lambda in the similarity score
        reg_alpha         = 0.0,       # L1
        subsample         = 0.8,       # rows per tree
        colsample_bytree  = 0.8,       # columns per tree
        scale_pos_weight  = (ytr == 0).sum() / (ytr == 1).sum(),  # imbalance
        tree_method       = "hist",    # histogram binning -> fast
        eval_metric       = "auc",
        early_stopping_rounds = 50,
        n_jobs            = 4,
        random_state      = 0)

clf.fit(Xtr, ytr, eval_set=[(Xtr, ytr), (Xte, yte)], verbose=False)
print("best_iteration:", clf.best_iteration)
print("test AUC      :", round(roc_auc_score(yte, clf.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]), 4))

# the learning curves that early stopping used
hist = clf.evals_result()
print("final train logloss/auc:", hist["validation_0"]["auc"][-1])

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. MISSING VALUES -- NO IMPUTER NEEDED
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
rng  = np.random.default_rng(0)
Xtrm = Xtr.copy(); Xtrm[rng.random(Xtr.shape) < 0.2] = np.nan
Xtem = Xte.copy(); Xtem[rng.random(Xte.shape) < 0.2] = np.nan

m = xgb.XGBClassifier(n_estimators=300, tree_method="hist",
                      missing=np.nan, n_jobs=4).fit(Xtrm, ytr)
print("AUC with 20% NaN:",
      round(roc_auc_score(yte, m.predict_proba(Xtem)[:, 1]), 4))

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. THE NATIVE API + BUILT-IN CROSS VALIDATION  ("cv is built in")
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
dtrain = xgb.DMatrix(Xtr, label=ytr)
dtest  = xgb.DMatrix(Xte, label=yte)

params = {"objective": "binary:logistic", "eval_metric": "auc",
          "eta": 0.05, "max_depth": 5, "lambda": 2.0, "gamma": 0.5,
          "subsample": 0.8, "colsample_bytree": 0.8,
          "tree_method": "hist", "nthread": 4}

cv = xgb.cv(params, dtrain,
            num_boost_round      = 2000,
            nfold                = 5,
            stratified           = True,
            early_stopping_rounds= 50,
            seed                 = 0,
            verbose_eval         = False)
best_rounds = len(cv)
print("cv says use", best_rounds, "rounds; mean AUC",
      round(cv["test-auc-mean"].iloc[-1], 4))

booster = xgb.train(params, dtrain, num_boost_round=best_rounds)
print("held-out AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(yte, booster.predict(dtest)), 4))

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. INSPECTING THE MODEL
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 'gain' = average loss reduction from splits on that feature -- the honest one.
gain = booster.get_score(importance_type="gain")
top  = sorted(gain.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:5]
print("top features by gain:", [(k, round(v, 1)) for k, v in top])

# Dump the first tree as text -- you can read the split thresholds,
# the leaf weights w = -G/(H+lambda), and the 'missing' default branch.
print(booster.get_dump()[0][:400])

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. REGRESSION IS THE SAME OBJECT
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
Xr, yr = make_regression(n_samples=3000, n_features=15, noise=10, random_state=0)
Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(Xr, yr, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
reg = xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=1000, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=4,
                       reg_lambda=2.0, subsample=0.8, tree_method="hist",
                       early_stopping_rounds=40, n_jobs=4)
reg.fit(Xa, ya, eval_set=[(Xb, yb)], verbose=False)
print("R2:", round(reg.score(Xb, yb), 4), "at", reg.best_iteration, "rounds")
Everything on one page
Summary

Same loop, better tree. XGBoost is gradient boosting where each tree is
grown to minimise a second-order approximation of the actual loss plus an
explicit penalty, instead of a generic MSE-on-residuals criterion.
Three formulas are the whole method:

w^\star_j=-\frac{G_j}{H_j+\lambda},\qquad
\text{Sim}_j=\frac{G_j^2}{H_j+\lambda},\qquad
\text{Gain}=\text{Sim}_L+\text{Sim}_R-\text{Sim}_{\text{parent}}-\gamma .
For squared loss $\text{Sim}=\frac{(\sum r)^2}{n+\lambda}$ — the notes' version.

Tuning order that works: fix a low learning_rate (0.05) and a
large n_estimators with early stopping $\to$ tune max_depth and
min_child_weight $\to$ tune subsample/colsample_bytree
$\to$ tune gamma/reg_lambda $\to$ finally lower the learning rate
once more and refit.
Interview corner
Q. What does XGBoost add over plain gradient boosting?

Second-order (Newton) optimisation instead of first-order, regularisation
written into the objective so leaf weights and split gains are shrunk, a
learned default direction for missing values, $\gamma$-based pruning on the
gain, histogram binning and column blocks for speed, and built-in CV with early
stopping.
Q. Derive the optimal leaf weight.

Taylor-expand the loss to second order, group rows by leaf, and you get
$G_j w_j + \frac12(H_j+\lambda)w_j^2$ per leaf. Differentiate and set to zero:
$w_j^\star=-G_j/(H_j+\lambda)$. Substituting back gives the similarity score
$G_j^2/(H_j+\lambda)$.
Q. Boosting is sequential — so what exactly is parallelised?

Not the boosting rounds. Within a single tree, the search for the best split
across features (and across bins within a feature) is parallelised, using
pre-sorted column blocks. Prediction is also parallel.
Q. What is min_child_weight?

The minimum sum of Hessians in a child. For squared loss $h_i=1$, so it is just
a row count. For log loss $h_i=p_i(1-p_i)$, so it is a count weighted by
uncertainty — a leaf full of confidently-predicted rows contributes almost
nothing and will not be split further. It is a smarter
min_samples_leaf.
Q. What is $\gamma$ and how is it different from max_depth?

max_depth is a hard structural cap applied before any split is
evaluated. $\gamma$ is a price: a split must buy at least $\gamma$ of gain to
survive. XGBoost grows to max_depth and then prunes back any branch
whose gain did not clear $\gamma$, so a deep-but-worthwhile branch can survive
even when a shallow-but-worthless one is cut.
Q. Why does XGBoost not need imputation?

Each split learns which way missing rows should go, chosen to maximise gain.
Missingness often carries signal (a blank income field is not random), and
mean-imputing would destroy it while also inventing values that never occur.
Q. Which feature importance should I trust?

None of the three fully — weight counts split frequency and inflates
high-cardinality features, cover counts rows touched, gain
measures loss reduction and is the best default. For decisions that matter,
use permutation importance or SHAP, which are model-output based rather than
structure based.
Q. Handling class imbalance in XGBoost?

scale_pos_weight = n_negative / n_positive reweights the gradients
of the positive class. Evaluate with AUC or average precision, not accuracy,
and remember it changes calibrated probabilities.
